# Atlas: Every AI tool you use should know how your company works

Your company has house rules. Now every AI tool follows them.

Published June 26, 2026

[Visit official site↗](https://atlas.nanonets.ai/?utm_source=chatgate&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=post_page)

![Atlas: Every AI tool you use should know how your company works](https://cdn.chatgate.ai/post/2026/06/atlas.png)

Atlas is a Nanonets product that turns company rules, process knowledge, data definitions, and brand context into a shared layer for everyday AI tools. The official [Atlas site](https://atlas.nanonets.ai/) says teams can set up their company context once, then use it from Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex, or custom agents, while the [Product Hunt launch](https://www.producthunt.com/products/nanonets) summarizes the idea as: every AI tool should know how your company works.

## What context does Atlas try to capture?

Atlas focuses on the repeated explanations teams already paste into AI tools: how internal processes work, where data lives, what metrics mean, and what on-brand output should look like. On [atlas.nanonets.ai](https://atlas.nanonets.ai/), Nanonets describes three layers: process context, data context, and brand context. Process context answers questions like internal access flows; data context explains schemas and metric definitions; brand context gives agents the fonts, colors, and design rules needed for decks, images, and copy.

The setup is intentionally pragmatic. Atlas says users can point it at a website, employee handbook, brand guide, documents, and optionally Notion, then review the extracted context on a single page. That fits Nanonets' existing company story: the main [Nanonets site](https://nanonets.com/) describes the broader platform as AI agents for enterprise data processing, built to automate messy manual processes and deliver clean data into business systems. Atlas applies that extraction muscle to company memory rather than invoices or logistics documents.

## How does Atlas connect to the tools people already use?

Atlas is not trying to become another chat UI. Its value depends on portability. The official [Atlas page](https://atlas.nanonets.ai/) says teams can plug one MCP URL into Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, and Claude Code, use one REST endpoint for custom agents, and export the rules as plain markdown to avoid lock-in. That is important because AI adoption inside companies is fragmented: one teammate may write in ChatGPT, another codes in Cursor, and another uses Claude for analysis.

The technical bet aligns with the Model Context Protocol. The official [MCP documentation](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/getting-started/intro) defines MCP as an open standard for connecting AI applications to external systems such as files, databases, tools, and workflows. Anthropic's [MCP announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol) describes the same goal as secure, two-way connections between data sources and AI-powered tools. Atlas uses that pattern for a narrower business problem: make company context reusable across models instead of trapped in one prompt thread.

## Who is Atlas built for?

Atlas says it is built for the "10-to-50 stage," where every employee may already use Claude, Cursor, and ChatGPT, but no one has time to re-explain onboarding flows, brand rules, or metric definitions every time. That makes it most relevant to startups and small teams with enough internal knowledge to create confusion, but not enough process maturity to justify a heavy knowledge-management rollout.

The [Product Hunt launch](https://www.producthunt.com/products/nanonets) also matters because Atlas is launching under an established Nanonets product profile rather than as a standalone experiment. Nanonets' [document parsing and extraction page](https://nanonets.com/document-parsing-and-extraction) says its APIs convert complex documents into structured data for use cases including RAG pipelines, and its [security policy](https://legal.nanonets.com/security-policy) states that Nanonets is SOC 2 compliant and ISO/IEC 27001 certified, with SOC 2 Type I and Type II reports available under NDA. Buyers still need to run their own security review, but the vendor is not starting from zero.

External coverage is still early. The Product Hunt [Leaderboard newsletter](https://www.producthunt.com/newsletters/archive/51972-bring-your-own-brain) describes Atlas as a portable context graph built on Nanonets' document-extraction engine, while a [Comparateur-IA Nanonets review](https://comparateur-ia.com/en/reviews/nanonets) independently frames Nanonets as a document-intelligence and AI-agents platform for automating workflows around unstructured documents.

## What are the limitations and buying questions?

Atlas should help most when a company has clear source material: handbooks, onboarding docs, brand guides, data dictionaries, product docs, and working process notes. If the company knowledge is mostly tribal, contradictory, or out of date, Atlas may make that mess more visible before it makes the AI better. Teams should also decide who owns the shared company layer, because the [Atlas page](https://atlas.nanonets.ai/) distinguishes personal context from admin-curated company context.

Pricing is visible at launch: Atlas lists early access at $99 per month per company for the first 200 companies, with no payment upfront and white-glove setup included. The practical next step is to collect a small set of source documents, connect Atlas to one or two AI tools, and test whether answers about process, data, and brand become more accurate than a well-maintained manual system prompt.
